analysis.one_liner: Caps the total cost federal regulations can impose on businesses each year, with the cap set by Congress.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap federal regulatory costs was referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee in March 2014 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new White House-adjacent office to count what federal rules cost the businesses and governments they apply to, and then required Congress to pass an annual "regulatory budget" setting a dollar cap on those costs for the government as a whole and for each agency. Any agency that hit its cap would have been barred from issuing new rules that raise costs, and any rule issued over the cap could be voided in court. In effect, it would have made the cost of regulation the main yardstick for whether protections get adopted, regardless of what they deliver in safety, health, or savings.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that bear the cost of federal rules — manufacturers, energy companies, financial firms, and other regulated industries — would gain a hard ceiling on new compliance costs. The bill would also give any party standing to sue and strike down a rule issued over the cap, a powerful tool for delaying or killing regulations.

how_it_helps.text: Congress would have to pass an annual National Regulatory Budget setting an overall cost cap and a separate cap for each executive agency, with the first budget taking effect in fiscal 2016 [S2][S3].

An agency that exceeds its annual cost cap could not issue any new rule that increases regulatory costs until it is back under the cap, and a rule issued in violation would have no force or effect, enforceable by any party in federal district court [S2][S3].

A new independent Office of Regulatory Analysis would publish a cost analysis of every proposed major rule (those imposing $25 million or more in annual costs) and could delay a rule from taking effect for at least 75 days after the analysis is done [S2][S3].
Agencies that fail to hand over information to the new office within 45 days would face an automatic cut of half of one percent of their appropriations, enforced through sequestration [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public pays in the form of protections that never get adopted: whenever an agency's cap is full, new worker-safety, consumer-protection, environmental, or public-health rules would be blocked no matter how large their benefits, because the bill counts only what rules cost and never what they save. Federal agencies also lose funding for slow cooperation, and state and local governments are counted among the "regulated entities" whose costs fill the caps.

drawbacks.text: The bill counts only the costs of regulation and sets the caps on that number alone; it creates no comparable accounting of benefits, so a rule preventing deaths or illness would count against an agency while its gains would not count for it [S2][S3].

A one-size cap treats very different rules alike: an agency at its cap could not issue a new health or safety rule that costs money even in an emergency short of a formal public-health exception, and the 75-day waiting period would delay protections even in normal cases [S3].

Letting any party sue to void a rule issued over the cap would invite years of litigation over cost estimates, which are uncertain by nature, adding legal uncertainty for businesses and agencies alike [S3].

Supporters' honest case: regulatory costs are real, fall hardest on small businesses, and are currently never totaled anywhere in the budget process, so making Congress vote on a cap would force an explicit tradeoff. The counterweight is that the bill's design weights that tradeoff entirely toward cost by ignoring benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real problem — nobody totals the cost of regulation — but its design answers that problem in one direction only: costs are counted, benefits are not, and once an agency's cap is full, new protections are simply prohibited. For the public, the likely cost in foregone safety, health, and consumer protections would outweigh the gain in reduced compliance spending, which would flow overwhelmingly to the largest regulated firms. Better-designed cost accounting without a hard cap could capture most of the upside with far less of the downside.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Marco Rubio introduced the National Regulatory Budget Act of 2014 on March 25, 2014, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs [S1][S5].
Twelve Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote — the referral was the bill's last action before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, agencies kept the ability to issue new protections without a congressional cost cap, and regulated industries did not get the ceiling on compliance costs or the litigation tool the bill would have created. Supporters of a regulatory budget gained nothing but a floor statement of principle.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulated industries gained nothing; rulemaking authority stayed unchanged

for.name: Sen. Marco Rubio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Regulatory Budget Act of 2014 and was its sole sponsor.

for.name: 12 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: Sen. Tom Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after it was referred to his committee; the record shows no committee action of any kind.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 12 cosponsors were Republicans, and with Democrats holding the Senate majority and the Homeland Security chairmanship, the bill never advanced past referral.

industries.industry: Regulated businesses (manufacturers, energy, finance, and other rule-bound industries)
industries.note: The bill would cap the total compliance costs agencies can impose on these entities and void rules issued over the cap, directly reducing their regulatory burden. The cost of that relief falls on the public in the form of protections that never get issued, since the caps count costs but not benefits.

Small firms bear disproportionate compliance costs and would gain from caps and from annual reporting on regulatory costs to small businesses. But small businesses also rely on public protections (safety standards, fair-lending rules), which the caps would block alongside rules that burden large firms.

Agencies would lose control over how much regulation they issue, face an automatic half-percent appropriations cut for slow cooperation with the new office, and see new rulemaking blocked once caps were hit. This would constrain agencies' ability to respond to public-health, safety, and market problems.

industries.industry: State and local governments and nonprofits
industries.note: They are counted as regulated entities, so rules imposing costs on them would fill the caps and they would benefit from fewer costly mandates. That benefit comes at the price of weaker federal standards they and their residents may rely on.
